FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO RECOVER
speechtext: What assistance or measures to assist are furnished by the Department of Agriculture, to a farmer or other producer who, having shipped hogs to a packer, has received less than the floor price then prevailing, to recover the difference between the amount received and the existent floor price?

maintopic: FEDERAL ASSISTANCE TO RECOVER
speechtext:
The fact is that up to date we have had nothing to indicate that that has happened. I have before me now the answer to the statement brought in by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort which I think is the explanation of the situation as it exists and what is done with regard to it. I shall, as indicated, return that statement to him, having read this to the house.
The hogs referred to in the attached statement were apparently delivered direct to the packing plant where they were purchased for $18.75 as compared with a floor price of $19 which applies to public stockyards in Saskatoon. It will be noted that the trucker passed the stockyards on his way to the packing plant and therefore chose the market where, in his opinion, he would receive the better price. The price received, however, does not appear to be out of line with the floor price of $19 on the stockyards as he was able to unload his hogs at the plant without any expense, whereas if they had been marketed through the stockyards he would have had to pay for such services as are required in connection with the sale of hogs on public stockyards, which could easily absorb the 25-cent differential. The price at plants is quite commonly somewhat below the stockyard price.
The application of the support price is only practical at public yards where there is competitive buying and those who wish to be assured of support prices can, in cases like

Questions
this, deliver their hogs to the public stockyards. They are, however, at liberty to sell direct if they believe they will get better returns. In doing so, they assume responsibility and may, in some cases, get a better price and in some cases they may lose. There does not, however, appear to have been a deviation from the support price through this private sale.
Those are the facts in connection with this one sale and variations of those facts would be the case in connection with others. However, the fact is that this gentleman could have taken his hogs to the stockyard at Saskatoon and have received $19, but he thought he would do better and took them directly to the packing plant where he received 25 cents less, which means that he himself was satisfied he would get a better floor price there than he would if he had delivered to the yards.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 17 the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) asked the following questions:
Are there any negotiations under way at the present time, either with the United States government or with the provinces concerned, arising out of the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway, in which questions are being raised as to protection of property bordering on the lakes? If so. what steps are being taken on behalf of the Canadian
Inquiries of the Ministry government to see that Canadian land on the lakes is being properly protected against change of water levels?
I should point out that in the international joint commission order of approval of October 29, 1952, concerning the power developments in the St. Lawrence river, the following provision was inserted about protection to property owners who might be injured by the resultant change of levels of lake Ontario:
All interests on either side of the international boundary which are injured by reason of the construction, maintenance and operation of the works shall be given suitable and adequate protection and indemnity in accordance with the laws in Canada or the constitution and laws in the United States respectively, and in accordance with the requirements of article VIII of the treaty.
That is the boundary waters treaty.
Recently, as the house knows, the governments of Canada and the United States approved the recommendations of the international joint commission on the range of elevations of lake Ontario to be put into effect when the works in the St. Lawrence river are completed. In approving these recommendations the government was satisfied that this range of elevations, which is made possible by the St. Lawrence power project, far from being injurious to property owners on lake Ontario will in fact give them some protection against extreme high and low levels which they have not enjoyed heretofore. Nevertheless, the question of suitable legal redress for the property owners who might be injured as a result of the approval of the international joint commission recommendation has been raised by interested parties on both sides of the international boundary. Consequently both Canada and the United States are examining the adequacy of legal redress for injured interests as described in the international joint commission order and exchanges are now taking place between the two governments. In addition, since this legal redress falls partly within the jurisdiction of the provinces, consultations with provincial authorities will take place.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, February 17, consideration of the motion of Mr. Howe (Port Arthur) for the second reading of Bill No. 82, to provide for short-term credit to grain producers in the prairie provinces to meet temporary financial difficulties arising from inability to deliver all their grain, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Nicholson.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last Friday afternoon I was making the point that, in contrast to the position of the United States in relation to the critical situation in the grain trade, Canada was doing comparatively little. In support of that viewpoint, I merely have to quote the title of the bill we have been discussing for some time now, Bill 82, which suggests that the problem facing the wheat producers is only a temporary problem which requires merely temporary financial assistance as provided in the bill before us. I would like to disagree with that viewpoint as strongly as possible.
Up to the present moment, other than the bill we have before us, there has been no action on the part of the government to deal with the problem. Admittedly, we shall have Bill 83 before us within the next few days but, with reference to the position of the United States and its aggressive sales policy, we have had only mild reprimands from this government. Another possible solution has been put forward, and that is the possibility of some national disaster such as a drought that would automatically solve the surplus problem with which we are faced at the moment.
It would seem that the government has decided to adopt what might be called a status quo approach to this difficulty, and that, of course, is indicated by statistics that are available concerning Canadian participation in world wheat marketing in the past ten years. While the pattern has been changing considerably and the United States has been

moving into that area aggressively, we have continued to participate in the world wheat market only to the extent of some 30 per cent.
It must also be recalled that during the immediate post-war years we benefited considerably, by way of exports to the European market, from the extensive United States Marshall aid program that was proceeding after the end of world war II. Now that the Americans have moved toward a surplus crop disposal program of their own, that particular source of export has tended to decline.
Canada is going to be faced this year with very important decisions concerning international wheat trading, and uncertainty in this regard has already been indicated by our attitude towards the international wheat agreement. Perhaps, if we had been more flexible in our negotiations when this arrangement was last up for consideration, Canada would be in a much more favourable position in the world wheat market at the present time. During recent days the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) has indicated that the export possibilities for wheat in the world market are quite hopeful, and a potential figure of some 320 million bushels has been quoted as the total export figure for Canadian grain.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot allow that figure to go on the record unchallenged. That is the figure of total deliveries last year, and, if anybody has quoted it as export sales, it must have been a member of the opposition. Certainly no member of the government has quoted it as the figure for exports.

maintopic: PROVISION FOR GUARANTEE OF BANK LOANS TO PRODUCERS IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES, ETC.

speechtext:
Then I will change the terminology. I will admit that I am not a practical farmer at the moment, although I am descended from a long line of farmers. However, I would say that I have had as much practical farm experience as has the minister. He tends to discredit my experience in that regard but I do not think it is necessary for us to be practical participating farmers in order to make a contribution to this important discussion. The matter affects more than the farm economy directly. It affects more than the farmers directly. In fact, it involves very intimately-and I think the minister will agree with this statement- not only our western economy but our total Canadian economy and it has world-wide implications as well.
I should now like to come back to the point I was making, namely that there is a possibility that we shall market 320 million bushels of wheat by the end of the current year. That is something that is to be hoped for, of course, because it would ease to a certain extent the mounting crisis in the wheat economy. However, I think it can be demonstrated that even if we market in those optimistic amounts, we shall still have a surplus of some 600 million bushels of wheat in Canada at the beginning of the next crop year.
I had better document that statement for the sake of the record. I can do so by projecting some figures into the future. We have at the present time, or at least as of January 11 of this year, 797-5 million bushels of grain available. The estimated domestic utilization between January 12 and July 31 of this year, which will be the end of the crop year, can be projected at 30 million bushels. That is estimated on a total average domestic consumption of some 60 million bushels. Estimated exports of wheat and wheat flour from winter ports from mid-January to mid-April can be estimated at 60 million bushels and, from the opening of navigation to July
31, at some 105 million bushels. Hence the total estimated disappearance from January 11 to July 31 of this year will be something like 195 million bushels. Subtracting that figure from the total available supply at the moment of 797-5 million bushels, we find it leaves us with a surplus of 602-5 million bushels. That is a sizeable carryover in any one crop year and that statement is all on the basis of the optimistic marketing figure of 320 million bushels. This problem is therefore not temporary, Mr. Speaker; it is a continuing problem and it must be met by more substantial and vigorous policies than those which have been enunciated by the minister up to the present time.
There is another point to be considered in connection with this matter of the sale of grain. During recent months we have had an increase in the export marketings of grain. That is largely owing to the fact that we have had to drop, by substantial margins, the price of our lower qualities or lower grades of grain. If that had been done before, perhaps we would have been able to clear the low quality grain that was clogging our distribution system and thus would have been in a happier position today. But since last August, for example, No. 5 grade, which was then $1.49 per bushel, has decreased in price to $1.22 per bushel. That was at December. No. 6 grade has decreased in price from $1.47 in August to $1.18 in December and feed grain has decreased from $1.44 to $1.14. The result is that the demand for that lower grade grain has considerably increased and is largely responsible for the increased marketings during recent months, including the special arrangements with countries behind the iron curtain.
I should like to bring to the attention of the house another point which is sometimes missed. We are concerned not only with the problem of wheat. It must also be noted that other coarse grains including barley, oats and rye, exports are down for the past few months. For example, the figure for barley is 13 million bushels behind that of the previous year and for oats it is 15 million bushels behind. On top of that we have our perpetual box car situation. All of these circumstances tend to suggest that the prairie grain farmer is going to find himself in distress for some considerable time ahead. This means that the government must take much more strenuous steps than it has already indicated in any legislation we have before us.
This point was summed up by the twentieth century research fund project on the grain problem in North America, which incidentally included a Canadian, namely Dr. Andrew Stewart, president of the University of

Grain
Alberta. Dr. Stewart at the present time is serving as a member of the Gordon commission which is dealing with Canada's general economic position and its prospects for the future. In summing up this long-term problem of agriculture and in summing up the problem of the crisis with respect to grain, we must remember that it is basically a North American problem. Canada and the United States are producing tremendous surpluses which have caused the glut on the world market. Among many other conclusions, the twentieth century fund researchers came to this conclusion, which I think emphasizes the point I am trying to make at the present time:
. . . we recommend that effective aid be given to individual farmers in working out the kinds of changes in farming that will enable them, with as little hardship as possible, to make the adjustment that apparently will have to be made in the not distant future whatever kind of program is adopted. Where such adjustments put a severe strain on the resources and income of the farmers concerned, we favour liberal aid in the form of special credits and, if necessary, special payments during the transition period.
The twentieth century fund researchers, after looking exhaustively at the problem from all its aspects, came to the conclusion that there was a critical situation in our agricultural economy. They came to the conclusion that during the transition period-it is not a temporary thing-the maximum assistance would have to be given to the farmer by way of professional advice on diversifying his economy and solving his economic difficulties as well as by way of direct credit and cash extensions to him. That, of course, is contrary to a lot of the traditional economic thinking on the North American continent but in both the United States and Canada the role of government in the marketing of grain and in agricultural policy generally has become very firmly established during the past 20 years, and because of the situation as it exists at the moment the Canadian government has to take very vigorous action to deal with the difficulty.
I say that obviously we are being presented with the traditional Liberal policy that has often been referred to as hope and grope, hoping that everything will work out for the best, waiting for something to happen that will be in the best interests not of the people of Canada but of the party in power. That has been the policy followed by the present administration since the end of world war II, and long before. At the end of the war we were preparing for a depression. We were gearing ourselves for a depression. That was the advice of all economists. In our attempts to stave off the anticipated depression we ran into inflationary conditions, and I would point out that inflation is one of the

basic causes for the grain producer's difficulties at the present time. He is caught in the cost-price squeeze as a result of continuing inflationary pressures in Canada.
Notwithstanding the anticipated depression, Canada, because of her changed position in the world economy, because of the devastated European markets and because of the unanticipated demands for consumer goods and so forth, moved into an era of prosperity and the administration immediately took credit for that period of prosperity. I remember that in 1953 the slogan was, "Keep Canada Prosperous, Vote Liberal". The prairie farmer is not enjoying that prosperity for some of the reasons I have pointed out and for reasons that other speakers have mentioned in this debate. It is a difficult, complex, economic problem. It is related to the situation with which the west has been confronted under all the long years of Liberal administration, namely, an underdeveloped economy, and an attempt to play off the east against the west on the basis of bogus issues such as free trade versus protection and so on.
I was interested in a newspaper dispatch concerning the speech by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) last Saturday to the Liberal students federation in which he said that the Conservatives were responsbile for speaking with two voices in Canada. That particular point might go over on the hustings, but it certainly will not go over with a group of university students because we now have available in Canada very excellent political histories.
For one I could mention the excellent work on the life of John A. Macdonald that has recently been completed by Professor Creighton of the University of Toronto which puts a lot of the political history of Canada into its correct perspective. Our university students are reading these political histories. Fact is being sorted out from fiction, propaganda from history, and it is being discovered that more than one political party in Canada has made outstanding contributions to the national development of our country. I could mention other works such as "The Age of Mackenzie King" or even Bruce Hutchison's book, "The Incredible Canadian", which refers to a former Liberal prime minister as the Blondin of politics, indicating an ability to juggle precariously on both sides of the political tightrope.
To sum up my remarks, the point is that nothing is being done in a positive way to deal with the critical agricultural situation facing Canada and the United States. It is essentially a North American problem, and if we are going to solve it we must go much

Grain
further than the bill we have before us in order to deal with it adequately over the next decade or two. A balance must be restored between production and consumption. Healthy trading relations must also be established because wheat in North America depends upon a thriving export market for its continued prosperity.
Just a few moments ago we had an example of the hope and grope policy. The Minister of Trade and Commerce was asked if it was the intention to do anything about the unfavourable balance of trade that Canada has with the United States, and the answer was no. That, Mr. Speaker, is not good enough, and I am sure the people of Canada will readily come to that conclusion. In solving this problem changes will have to take place step by step. There are no easy overnight solutions and these changes as they come step by step will have to be made in the right direction. I submit that the measure now before us does not move in the right direction but is rather a retrograde step.

Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the house have been taunted many times about not getting up and speaking, but for the last week I have been trying to get the floor and every time I did somebody got ahead of me. Therefore, I have been left over until today. It has been said many times in the house that we in the centre of this country are not interested in the farmers' plight. I should like to say, Mr. Speaker, that we are not only interested in the farmers' plight but we are in great sympathy with the farmer. We believe it is in the interest of all Canada that the farmer be prosperous. If the farmer is not prosperous, then there is very little prosperity in the country. It is my belief that we should help him in times of depression and whenever a need arises. But, Mr. Speaker, there is a limit to the help that we should give to the farmer. Should we go beyond common sense, or should we help him whether he needs it or not?
The hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) told us the other day that in his province many of the farmers own farms greater in area than the whole state of Israel. Surely, Mr. Speaker, you could not consider him a poor farmer or a farmer in need of help. If he owns that amount of land and cultivates it, he has ample opportunity in the good years to put aside something for a rainy day.
It is the duty of the government to help the farmers, as I have said, and I am sure the government is very anxious to help them and to see that they receive their fair share of the revenue of Canada. But surely the
intelligent farmer, as he is-we all recognize that the farmers on the prairies are very intelligent men because they have prospered to a great extent during the last few years- has put aside a reasonable amount of money. Not all of them need help; perhaps some do. We have been told that there are around
200.000	farmers in the west. Surely, 150,000 of those do not need help. If the government were to guarantee loans to farmers, irrespective of whether they have money or not, those 200,000 farmers would be able to obtain guaranteed government loans without any interest. What would be the result? We all know that the majority of farmers as well as the industrialists and everyone else have some collateral. They hold mortgages, bonds, stocks, that they can call on for a rainy day. If no interest was charged on those loans and 50,000 farmers needed help, and the loans were guaranteed to everyone, the 150,000 farmers who did not need help would surely be foolish if they did not take advantage of the government guaranteed loan. Those
150.000	farmers, whether they needed it or not, would go to the bank and secure a loan of $1,500 without any interest, and then they would invest that money in stocks or bonds or mortgages, and they would be drawing interest of $75 a year.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal briefly with the basic reason why this government finds itself in such an unholy mess today with regard to wheat sales. The simple reason is that the government's selling efforts have been inadequate and utterly pathetic. To show what this government has done in the way of

making export shipments of wheat as compared with what has been done by other countries, I intend to quote some dominion bureau of statistics figures. The following are the export shipments of wheat and wheat flour in terms of wheat expressed in millions of bushels by the five leading exporting countries during the 1953-54 crop year:
Canada	 255 1
Australia	 63-4
France	 34-0
Argentina	  110-3
United States	 211-4
The following are the export shipments in millions of bushels for the crop year immediately past:
Canada	 251-8
Australia	 94-2
France	 83-8
Argentina	 134-5
United States	 276-5
Those figures show that Canada shipped 3 [DOT] 3 million bushels less for a decrease of 1 [DOT] 3 per cent. Australia increased her shipments by 30-8 million bushels for an increase of 48 [DOT] 6 per cent. France increased her shipments by 50 million bushels for an increase of 250 per cent. Argentina increased her shipments by 24-2 million bushels for an increase of 21-9 per cent, and the United States increased its shipments by 65-1 million bushels for an increase of 30-8 per cent.
What that adds up to is that the four other major exporters of wheat shipped 170 million bushels more during the last crop year than during the crop year immediately preceding, for an increase of 40 per cent, while in the case of Canada, the shipments decreased 3 [DOT] 3 million bushels or 1 [DOT] 3 per cent. That performance has been carried into the first quarter of the present crop year when Canada shipped 14-2 million bushels less than in the same quarter of the preceding crop year, for a decrease of 19 per cent. In other words, all the other wheat exporting countries were able to ship 40 per cent more wheat than in the preceding year, while we shipped 1-3 per cent less.
I think that that is a disgraceful performance. The minister will quite likely say that the United States increased their shipments to a certain extent by adopting a giveaway program, and we will grant that. He will say that Argentina entered into barter agreements, and we will grant that. However, according to his own department, France and Australia, trading on the same basis as Canada, were able to ship 80 million bushels more during the past crop year than in the preceding crop year, while we shipped 3-3 million bushels less. In other words, France and Australia, trading on the same

Grain
basis as we do, seem to have salesmen who can go out and make sales. Canada just does not have that kind of salesmen.
What has happened is that during the war years and the later 1940's, while we were in a seller's market, this government became so used to sitting back and arrogantly expecting buyers to come to us that it has lost whatever sales technique it ever might have had. It certainly has none today, because other countries are making increased sales while we are making less sales. That is nothing less than a disgraceful performance.
What is required in any business to get additional sales, particularly when your competitors are getting additional sales, is that you first go and see your potential customers. You do not treat them with the arrogance with which this government has treated potential customers in the past. You get to know them and obtain their confidence. You sit down and talk to them. You say, "We have something to sell, and you need to buy our commodity. What kind of a deal can we engage in that will be mutually satisfactory?" By working back and forth, getting their confidence, getting to know them and being willing to sit down and work out a mutually satisfactory arrangement, finally a deal is consummated.
However, in the spring of 1953, while the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) and other hon. members urged the Minister of Trade and Commerce to go to England, when it was evident that Great Britain was not going to enter the international wheat agreement, and try to work out a mutually satisfactory arrangement with Great Britain, the minister said he was not interested in going, and he did not go. That simply exemplifies the attitude this government has taken towards the need for going out and selling a commodity which we must sell-because we have not sold it. We have tremendous stocks building up every day, and the farmers are asked to take the rap. They are asked to do what the members of the cabinet, I am sure, would refuse to do. It is the equivalent of the Minister of Finance making a muddle of his financial arrangements to such an extent that it is not possible to honour the pay cheques that members of the cabinet and members of parliament receive at the end of each month, and to their being required to go to the bank to borrow their salaries and pay five per cent on them. That is what this government is demanding that the farmers of this country do-something they know perfectly well they themselves would not be willing to do with regard to their own salaries. Payment for wheat is the salary that the wheat grower of this country receives.
The performance of this government with regard to selling wheat has resulted in a situation in which every other major competitor is showing an average increase of 40 per cent more shipments last crop year than this crop year, while we are showing less shipments. If that kind of performance were shown to any sales manager, it would result in the salesman being fired on the spot. It is about time the people of Canada, who are being so adversely affected by this mess that this government has got us into, should do the same thing and fire the salesman on whom we are relying to dispose of our wheat. I feel sure that the farmers of this country will look after that very important piece of business at the next election.

speechtext:
Mir. Speaker, it is rather fortunate that this afternoon we had a speaker on the government side of the house-the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Bourque)-giving us some figures about agricultural income. I would point out to him in all fairness that he would appreciate the position of the agricultural producers in western Canada a little better if he were to study some of the figures with regard to costs of operation and the decline in net income in his province as compared with those of the prairie producers. In his province, from 1952 to 1954, the farmers-most of them, I believe, are engaged in dairy production-had a reduction in their net income of about three per cent and they can still carry on. I can imagine what the situation would be like if the producers in his province suffered by a decline in net income of 77 per cent.
He suggested that, if these prairie producers were able to get this $1,500 in the west, most of them would be investing it in bonds and stocks and that kind of thing to take advantage of the government's offer of interest-free money, that it would be a bad thing for the rest of Canada and we could not expect them to support it. There could not be better proof of the lack of understanding of the situation or of the conditions under which those people are trying to exist and in which they have found themselves as a result of government policy.
The member who immediately preceded me, the hon. member for Broadview, made a very telling point. He showed rather conclusively that, because of the failure of this government to sell its wheat in the world's markets, other large wheat exporting countries were increasing their sales while Canada's sales were decreasing. It is the failure of the government to sell the grain that has caused the terminal elevators to be blocked up, the inland elevators to be filled,

Grain
the elevators at the delivery points to be filled and the farmers' bins now to be filled. In many cases, hundreds of thousands of bushels are lying out on the prairies without any covering at all for them. If this government accepts the principle of orderly marketing, it is up to it to purchase this grain.
I wish my hon. friend from Outremont-St. Jean and a good many other members on that side of the house would just try to appreciate that situation. Then perhaps they would not so blindly follow the government votes in this house.
This Bill 82 is supposed to provide shortterm credit for grain producers on the prairie provinces. The fact that it does not do so points up the bill-this is the best word I can use to describe it-as "phony". It does not do the job. To say the situation is a temporary financial difficulty the people are in, arising from an inability to deliver all their grain, carries with it the suggestion that most of the farmers are fairly well off and have delivered most of their grain. It is utterly impossible, I suppose, to get members here to understand the situation unless they will undertake to study it a little.
It is because this bill is wrong in principle, beause it does not do what the government has said it is going to do in the preamble or in the definition of the bill, that we are opposing it. If it provided cash to the farmer as a right, then perhaps there would be some reason for some of us to support it. The farmers' inability to deliver is directly the responsibility of this government. It is the failure of this administration to sell that grain, even to provide the box cars for the delivery of the grain at the points of delivery to fill the available space in the terminal elevators, that causes the people of the west to oppose it.
There are two great failures here, and they rest directly on the administration. If the government has failed in its responsibility and as a result has placed the producer in the position where he has not the money to pay his costs of operation for the past year and to pay his taxes and other operating expenses, then surely it is the government that should take the responsibility and should pay for that responsibility. It is misleading to say that this does take care of the situation. As a matter of fact, when the facts of the situation are known, it will be a disgrace to Canada if such a bill is placed on the statutes. I think we are doing the government a favour by suggesting to them that this is a disgraceful piece of legislation which purports to do something but which does not do it at all. Such a thing can only be described as being misleading. We have moved the six

months' hoist to this bill. We in this group are supporting that six months' hoist because behind the bill is a definite and real injustice.
Orderly marketing in principle implies responsibility on the part of those who are to purchase the grain. Under act of parliament-and rightly so-the wheat board is the sole agency for the purchase of this grain or at any rate by far the greater bulk of it. Orderly marketing also implies that it is the responsibility of the government to sell that grain. It is the responsibility of the transport controller and the boards under the government's direction to see that transportation facilities are available so that the farmer can deliver that grain to his local elevator and so that the grain can be shipped to terminals. The government has failed in those responsibilities and now, under this legislation, wishes to place a penalty on the producers, namely the penalty of extra debt and the penalty of extra interest. When the action of any one person causes harm to some other person the person who is guilty of causing the harm would, in a court of law and in the name of justice, be obliged to pay for that action. The damages of the plaintiff who complains against those who have caused him harm or loss would, in a court of justice, be assessed against the person causing that harm. In this case we have the government being responsible for the loss or harm suffered by the producer and the producer being penalized for the failure of the government to act. That is the basis upon which we refuse to accept this bill and upon which we condemn it as being unworthy of the government of Canada.
If we were to endorse this bill in any way we would be endorsing a principle which, if allowed to continue in the present maladministration, would place a continually increasing burden of debt and interest on the back of agriculture which could have only one ultimate result, namely to break it. The farmer is facing bankruptcy rapidly enough with constantly increasing costs of production and a decline in income. To put a further burden on him is further to condemn agriculture to poverty for years to come.
On numerous occasions over the past years we have suggested to this government that, with the situation developing as it was, it was their responsibility to provide storage in Canada for this grain which they must buy from the farmer. They have undertaken to buy it and they have undertaken to sell it. They must accept their responsibility to sell it. If they had built these inland elevators and provided for a food bank within Canada, it would have been for the good of all. Without that elevator space available, we are caught in the mess in which we find our producers today. If the government had carried out the

Grain
recommendations presented to them by this group on numerous occasions, they would have done a good deal to help and would have prevented the present situation entirely. They have failed to carry out those recommendations and they must accept the responsibility. If the government policy with regard to exchange, barter deals and their attitude towards other governments is responsible for the failure to sell grain, then the responsibility rests squarely on their shoulders.
Instead of tackling the problem, what do we find? They say, "Oh, if the farmer is in temporary difficulties, we will make arrangements whereby he can go to the bank and the bank will lend him money. We will guarantee that the banks do not lose anything"-at least we are guaranteeing up to 85 per cent, I believe, under the bill-"and you pay the interest on it. That is just a little extra burden." How far is this going to go? Where is the end of such a policy? Can we accept that principle? Surely we cannot do so. The bill being unjust and being without a proper basis in principle, we would be derelict in our duty, if we were to support it. We could not possibly do so.
It has been suggested that recognition of the justice of the case of the producer in the west, is limited to only a few people here and there. It is encouraging to find throughout Canada growing support for the justice of the case of the western producer in the predicament in which he finds himself today. Just a few days ago the leaders of the two great labour unions of Canada, representing organized labour in this country to the extent of almost one million people, issued a statement supporting the demands of the western farmer for cash advances on his farm-stored grain as a matter of right; and, even more significant, they are supporting the demands of organized agriculture throughout the whole of Canada for the establishment of a parity price, the only way in which the farmer can be assured of any security. With the costs of operation continuing to rise, he should be guaranteed a floor price which will bear a proper relationship to his costs of production. Without that parity price, he faces bankruptcy. Organized labour in Canada recognize that fact and have issued a statement supporting the demands of the farmer for that right.
The action of this government is completely ineffectual. This bill will not do the job; it cannot do the job. Why should it be presented to this house? Not only is it misleading and ineffectual but it is a travesty on justice. It is a burlesque imitation, of what should be done, and it is completely misleading.
Because it is useless and ineffectual, wrong in principle, dangerous to the future of agriculture and misleading, we are going to support the motion that 'the six months' hoist be given to this bill. That is our way of saying that it should not be passed by this house, that it should be thrown out and that something should be introduced which would restore the confidence of the people who are doing the job of producing the economic weapons in the struggle for men's minds today, the people who are producing and doing the job of producing the food that the world so desperately needs. The movement of people away from agriculture in this country can only mean that the army of people who provide probably the very basis upon which the good part of this country is built- the rural homes, the farm homes, the place from which our nation draws its strength- lack confidence.
One hon. member this afternoon compared what is happening in Canada to what has happened to agriculture in that great giant of a country to the south of us. Within the past few years the government of that country has supported agriculture with a parity price program. It recognizes that agriculture as of right deserves to be supported in an economy where the costs of operation, without price support, will mean the ruination of agriculture. They have spent some $799 million in support programs for agriculture. In spite of this fact, agriculture in that country still continues to decline. Here in Canada we have no such support. This government refuses to recognize the right of agriculture to any support prices when it is responsible for the increasing costs of living. With the costs of production continuing to rise, there must be some support for agriculture. The bill purports to deal with a matter of immediate importance, what amounts to a desperate situation, the shortage of cash in the prairie economy. It does not do the job and that is why we have moved an amendment to give the bill the six months' hoist. Basically it is only a part of the greater problem facing agriculture which we can discuss at another time. In refusing to recognize cash advances on grain properly stored on the farm, the government condemns the farmers of the country to a critical economic condition, but it also does more than that. Underlying the attitude of the government is a denial of the principle of orderly marketing, and only by the application of that principle is there any hope for the people of the prairie region and those of the rest of Canada engaged in the agricultural industry. I am pleased to support the amendment for the six months' hoist. I hope

Grain
that every hon. member, having studied the situation and knowing what he is voting for and what he is voting against, will do likewise.

speechtext:
Just a few minutes ago an hon. member said that the farmers of eastern Canada were opposed to this kind of thing. I do not believe the farmers of eastern Canada are opposed to cash advances in any way. As a matter of fact, just the other day one of the organizations representing the farmers of Ontario came into this building, met the various groups and advocated the very thing that we have been advocating, namely, cash advances. The Ontario farmers' union joined hands with the farmers' unions of the three prairie provinces in supporting cash advances and opposing bank loans.
This afternoon the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Bourque) said that the opposition members were pitting the farmers against the rest of Canada. When I said that members on the government side of the house were prepared to make statements that could in no way serve the cause of national unity, that was one of the statements I had in mind. I say that the people of Canada are not supporting the government in the action it has taken at this time. We in this group are not attempting to pit the farmers against the rest of Canada because we believe the majority of Canadians are fair and believe that agriculture from one end of this nation to the other is entitled to fair economic treatment and that the farmers are in fact entitled to an economic standard of living comparable with the rest of the nation.
What has the government said when we in this group have advocated measures such as

support prices in the interests of our farmers? They have said: You might be able to do something in this case but the consumer is against it and labour is against it. In other words, they say that the country is divided and that when the farmers want a certain policy the consumers are opposed to that policy. I do not believe that for a moment. I believe I can show that the nation as a whole is quite prepared to support the farmers in their demands for equity, justice, and for prices which will give them a reasonable standard of living.
We have seen the government attempt to divide farmers and labour. Because they have been able to do that with some success in the past, perhaps it has served their own ends. The Canadian Congress of Labour had a convention last fall and they came out in favour of 75 per cent cash advances on farm-stored grain. The labour unions are certainly far ahead of the government in advocating such a policy. Just a few days ago the farm-labour economic council issued a statement which was reported by the Canadian Press and is found in the Ottawa Journal of February 20. In it they had this to say:
Prairie farm unions, driving hard for cash advances on farm-held grain, now have powerful allies-spokesmen for some one million organized workers. The heads of the two national labour bodies, the Trades and Labour Congress and the Canadian Congress of Labour, Saturday agreed with farm unions that the need of such payments should be recognized.
T.L.C. chief Claude Jodoin and C.C.L. head A. R. Mosher, whose organizations are soon to amalgamate, agreed also that farmers should get "equitable" or parity prices on all farm products.
I say that statement is the best answer that could be given to the suggestion of the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean that we are attempting to pit the farmers against the rest of Canada. As a matter of fact, more and more it is becoming clear that the government's stand is in fact against the rest of Canada and that is the only division there is in the country on this question.
I have heard it said very frequently that farmers in eastern Canada, farmers in the maritimes and farmers in British Columbia do not support the policies that are advocated from time to time by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and other organizations speaking on behalf of the prairie farmers. I do not think that is true. Not only do I think that the farmers of the east and British Columbia are prepared to support reasonable demands advanced by prairie producers but I also believe that the prairie producers, as fair-minded Canadians, are prepared to support reasonable demands advanced by producers in all parts of Canada.

The hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Murphy), who is in his seat at the present time, made some very amazing statements in his contribution to this debate. Referring to the opposition he said, as found at page 971 of Hansard of February 8:
Why do they not come up with the same suggestion on wheat? Why do they not suggest that the government buy the wheat and give it to the Canadian public at such a low rate that bread will be a penny a loaf?
That is an open and public confession by the hon. member that he knows nothing about the grain business, that he knows nothing about the cost of the wheat that goes into a loaf of bread and knows very little about economics or he would not make the suggestion that bread, even if wheat were free, would come down to a penny a loaf. It might come down two, three, or three and a fraction cents a loaf but that is all because most of the cost of a loaf of bread is for something other than the flour content of the loaf.
Then the hon. member went on to criticize the western wheat producers in very strong language. He said:
It seems to me that the western wheat producer in this case is the man who holds the big stick . . .
He says that the wheat producer in the west is the man who holds the big stick. He does not hold a stick at all. He holds a lot of grain that he cannot sell. He is out of money and the only place where he can sell his grain is the Canadian wheat board. He believes the government that has taken responsibility for the functioning of the Canadian wheat board should also take the responsibility for providing money to the producer when he is unable to deliver his grain. If there is a big stick at all it is being held and wielded by the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). Because of the power he possesses in the government he has said to the western wheat producers, in spite of an almost unanimous request for cash advances, I will have nothing to do with it and I will oppose it. It is not the farmer in the west that is wielding the big stick; it is the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
I do not think the statements I have referred to do the hon. member for Westmorland any credit. Since he is a member of the legal profession and has had a good deal of training one would expect that he would not make such statements as these.

Even though the hon. member for Westmorland may take exception to what I am now saying, his statements were, in my opinion, not quite so bad as those made by the hon. member for Wellington South (Mr. Hosking). In the statements he made he showed that he had no understanding not only of the grain business but of the livestock business of this country. As recorded on page 1298 of Hansard, he was quite prepared to interrupt the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort (Mr. Bryson) when that hon. member was making the statement that unless the government took action the prairie farmer would be forced to produce more livestock. The hon. member for Wellington South said:
Your farmer will certainly do some work for a change.
That shows the abysmal ignorance of the hon. member for Wellington South. He had already made other statements along the same line before he made that statement. At page 1297 of Hansard he had this to say. He had been questioning the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort regarding the production of livestock and he asked this question.
Why have they not done so before?
He was referring to the western producers. The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort replied:
We were getting rid of some grain before.
To that the hon. member for Wellington South made this statement:
Because they were making so much money from their wheat they did not have to raise livestock, like the eastern farmers, to make a living.
I looked up the record in the dominion bureau of statistics agricultural statistics, and I found something that amazed me. I will admit that. I found on the farms in western Canada, as of the 1951 census, almost exactly the same number of cattle and calves as are on farms in eastern Canada, namely, in Ontario and Quebec. As a matter of fact, in that year on each farm in Ontario and Quebec there were 12-5 head of cattle. In the same year on the prairies there were 12-1 head on each farm. The statement of the hon. member for Wellington South is therefore inaccurate.

What other hon. members of this group have been endeavouring to say is that just so long as the government fails to take action to solve the problem of the farmer obtaining money for his grain there will stand an ever-present threat to the livestock industry across this nation of the western producer deciding that he has vastly to increase the number of livestock on his farm. Because we believe that such a thing can only further increase the misery of agriculture in this nation we have been pointing out the need for the government to take action to place money in the hands of the wheat producers. We can talk as we like on this subject; we can talk about cash advances that are so important, but the main thing finally will be to get the grain moved, to get the grain sold and to get money for the sale of the grain in the pockets of the producers.
We have been pointing out the fact that sales of grain in recent years have been going down. We have pointed out the fact that increased crops, because of new methods, are likely to add to the surplus rather than detract from it, unless the government should vastly increase the sales of grain; but we were surprised to learn, as I am sure the nation was, that according to the Minister of Trade and Commerce the trouble is not the matter of sales; the trouble is not the matter of giving cash advances or loans. The minister had this to say in the debate at page 603 of Hansard:
Our big problem now is not selling, but transportation. If deliveries of wheat by producers this crop year do happen to fall behind last year, it will be because rail transportation is not adequate to move grain forward quickly enough and thus clear space in country elevators.
We have heard alibis of all kinds, but this is the main alibi, this is the last alibi, that there is a transportation bottleneck; that there is a shortage of box cars; that sales are marvellous; they have been going up; but if the transport controller did his job-that is in fact what the minister was saying-and provided more box cars, then the whole marketing problem would not be nearly so difficult. The transport controller, who is supposed to be an authority on the control and movement of box cars, replied to this statement about three weeks ago, according to a Canadian Press dispatch of February 17. He had this to say:
Transport controller Roy W. Milner, whose powers parliament will be asked to renew for two years, said Thursday there is no shortage of box cars holding up prairie grain shipments.
The Canadian wheat board has made an estimate of how much grain it will want moved by April 15 and "we will have that grain moved before that date."
[Mr. Robichaud.l
I have heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce criticized in this house for the statements he has made from time to time. I have seen many hon. members rise in their places and attempt to argue against the Minister of Trade and Commerce and refute his statements, but this is the first time in my memory that a senior civil servant has gone to the press and said in fact, in so many words, the minister does not know what he is talking about. The Minister of Trade and Commerce says there is a big shortage of box cars; that is the bottleneck; that is the trouble in moving grain. The transport controller says there is no shortage of box cars holding up prairie grain shipments.

speechtext:
I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce what had happened to the 58 million bushels effective capacity which was not used, as reported in an answer in this house on January 20. He said he did not know. He did not know whether it was more or less. We need a lot more information. I would like to see the agriculture committee of this house called at an early date. I would like to see the minister present his case to that committee for saying that the great difficulty is the shortage of box cars, and then it would be very interesting to have the transport controller tell us why he makes the statement that there is no shortage of box cars. In the last session and the present one we have seen increasing evidence that the government has lost touch and that the cabinet is no longer able to effectively carry out its duties. This is more evidence of the fact that the government is not effectively carrying out its obligations to the people of this nation.
I would like to see the Minister of Trade and Commerce make a statement in the house and tell us what the facts really are and tell us who is right. Is the minister right or is the transport controller right? Whatever the answer may be this situation should be solved so that the greatest effective capacity possible will be used and grain will be kept in position without having to pay demurrage on ocean vessels waiting in port and so on so that we may take advantage of every possible sale.
Someone made a statement in this chamber the other day to the effect that farmers have already marketed their normal crop. This statement was made by someone who

had been listening to the Minister of Trade and Commerce but who had failed to get the gist of his remarks. Farmers' marketings on the prairies so far this crop year are very low. There has been a calamitous drop in farm marketings. Day after day hon. members from western Canada are receiving letters and resolutions following meetings that are called asking for increased quotas, for more box cars and for the opportunity to go out in thirty or forty below zero weather to open a road by removing the snow so that they can get a few bushels to market.
The statistics I hold in my hand show that this situation is in fact prevalent on the prairies. I have here a list of farmers' marketings from the period August 1 to February 1 for a number of years. The high year in recent years is the period 1952-53 when farmers from August 1 to February 1 marketed 286 million bushels of wheat. The next year marketings in the same period were 241 million bushels of wheat and in that period 1954-55 marketings of wheat had dropped to 135 million bushels. For the current period marketings are down to 111 million bushels. In other words, from this period in 1952-53 when farmers marketed at country elevators on the prairies 286 million bushels of wheat, there has been a drop to 111 million bushels.
It is because of the lack of marketing and because of the fact that marketings have been so drastically curtailed that meetings in western Canada are still being held asking the government to provide a system of cash advances.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce keeps telling us that sales are better but when we ask him in the house what the sales are he says, "I will not tell you, it is not public; but I know they are better, I know sales are up." We have to rely on export figures, but a sale is transferred into an export before too long and the latest figures on exports which have come to my office are for the period August 1, 1955, to February 8, 1956. These figures show exports were 97-4 million bushels, a drop of approximately 18 million bushels from the same period last year.
I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce is right in saying our sales are up, but if he is, he is going to be right this year whereas he was wrong many, many times last year when he told us in this house that marketings and sales were up and that the 8-bushel quota would be off the farms. In fact, he said that farmers would be able to market all their grain before the new crop was harvested.
There is a great need to make certain that our exports are increased. One cannot help but feel that, unless we are successful in obtaining a new international wheat agreement,
Grain
these figures I have used today and the optimistic statements the Minister of Trade and Commerce is now making will not prove to be correct and sales may in fact go down.
I was very disappointed to learn that Great Britain would not consider coming into a new international wheat agreement. The fact that Britain has said no to a new international wheat agreement is no excuse for the Canadian government to take the position the minister suggested it was taking on February 16 when he said it would not be prepared to enter a new international wheat agreement unless two-thirds of the wheat entering into the channels of commerce were provided for in that agreement. Even with Britain participating in an agreement, it is doubtful if we would have two-thirds of the wheat that is entering into the commercial channels of the world covered. We have an international wheat agreement at the present time. It is not what we would like it to be, but let no one think that it is not an important agreement or that it does not cover a vast quantity of wheat or that there are not many countries in the world who are signatories to the agreement. The guaranteed quantities under the present international wheat agreement which is still in operation are 395 million bushels, and while we have exported 97 [DOT] 4 bushels in the crop year to February 8 the report of the international wheat council shows that in the period August 1, 1955, to February 10, 1956, Canada sold 52,734,000 bushels under the current international wheat agreement.
In other words, with an agreement restricted as it is without Britain we have exported approximately half of our wheat so far this year under the terms of that international wheat agreement.
I regret the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that Canada, at least on February 16, is apparently not thinking in terms of supporting a new international wheat agreement even though it would cover a much smaller quantity of grain.
The minister this afternoon in answer to a question asked by me stated that I had always said he should take the advice of farm organizations and he said that is what he was doing; he was taking the advice of farm organizations. As a matter of fact, he is doing some of the things which are absolutely opposed to the statements of leaders in the farm movement. When he made the statement that Canada would not consider an agreement unless two-thirds of the wheat that is entering into the commercial channels of the world was covered, Mr. Alf Gleave, the vice president of the Saskatchewan

Grain
farmers' union, Mr. Stewart Thiessen, secretary of the Saskatchewan farmers' union, and Mr. Alex Gilliland, the wheat pool manager, questioned the wisdom of the minister's statement.
According to the Winnipeg Free Press of February 18 in a news item entitled, "Howe Stand on I.W.A. Criticized", Mr. Gleave had this to say:
Why send a negotiating team to Geneva, then three days before the meeting opens, lay down a policy which limits their powers of negotiation?
The minister says that he consults with the farm organizations and their leaders and listens to their representations but as a matter of fact, according to Mr. Gleave, the minister has not consulted with them at all and three days before the opening of the international wheat agreement negotiations the minister cuts the ground in large part from under the feet of the people who are to take part in the negotiations.

Any reference I have made to the wheat situation today and to marketing policies, any statistics I have quoted, have been right around the subject with which the Minister of Trade and Commerce dealt most adequately when he opened this discussion on

January 27. I was not endeavouring to extend the scope of the debate; I was merely making comments on the general statement which the minister made when we first began this discussion.
The Minister of Agriculture is not at all reluctant to make statements on wheat. I am glad he is not, and I congratulate him upon being ready to do that even though he is wrong and at times he must feel that he is wrong. That does not bother him. He goes out to meetings of all kinds, in eastern Canada and western Canada, and makes statements as to his version of the farmer's position, as to why bank loans are good enough, as to why the government is opposed to cash advances, as to why the minister himself is opposed to cash advances. I believe the minister might have a different idea and the government might have accepted a different policy if they had started from a correct instead of a wrong premise.
I should like to refer to the report of a speech made by the Minister of Agriculture which appeared in the Windsor Daily Star of Thursday, February 2. It is headed "Wheat in Bin likened to Farm Bank Account". If I had not known who was making this speech I would not have needed to read any more than that headline to have guessed that it was the Minister of Agriculture, because that is an old theme of his that wheat in the bin is like money in the bank.
I am sure that the Minister of Justice is prepared to say that the farmers of Minne-dosa and district do not believe that statement by the Minister of Agriculture? As a matter of fact the Minister of Trade and Commerce does not entirely believe it either, because he is bringing in something which he expects will provide farmers with some money in their bank accounts; but according to the Minister of Agriculture if you have wheat at home it is just as good as money in the bank. He cannot convince anybody of that. The minister was making this speech before a medical society, so he did not have many hecklers I suppose. The report reads:
Mr. Gardiner told the doctors he has been criticized tor earlier statements in that vein, "But X still say agriculture is making a pretty lair showing in Canada."
The fact is that the farmer today is in a worse cost-price position than he was when the Minister of Agriculture took over his present portfolio; the farmer is in a worse price-cost position today than he was 20 years ago. The minister stated that as far as he was concerned the farmer's position today was pretty fair. Then he went on to say:
Alter all, the best bank account a farmer can have is a bin of wheat. That's because he can't spend it.

The Minister of Agriculture apparently says, "Don't give the farmer any money; don't give him a bank account, but let him have some wheat and then stop him from selling it. Don't give him any money because after all it is good for him that he cannot spend it". Is it any wonder that the minister is running into trouble? Is it any wonder that we have a return such as the one tabled the other day for the hon. member for Prince Albert, containing many resolutions and petitions with signatures running into the thousands all saying that the Minister of Agriculture is wrong when he says that wheat in the bin is as good as money in the bank? They indicate that the farmers in fact want the government to do something that will transfer wheat in the bin into cash. The minister went on to say:

It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that a statement of this type made by a responsible individual such as this man should be given

some consideration, not only because of the fact that he was making it for himself but because he was apparently speaking for a good number of citizens in that community. But I also like to think that the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) are not just raising something for political purposes. I think the lives of people in Canada have been played with politically just a little bit too much, and that it is high time we got the full truth of the matter.
It is a simple matter to get that truth. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Trade and Commerce was shooting a broadside at the C.C.F. for having courageously and most effectively battled, for many days now, on behalf of the people who sent them to parliament. I know it is not good politics on my part, but I think it is good Canadianism to congratulate the members of the C.C.F. who have planned and carried on this battle for having done a good job and for being ready to continue to do that job.
May I say this so the C.C.F. will not have to take all the opprobrium; that if they had not got in and started to move amendments to the motion for second reading, the Social Credit group would have done it. The members of the Social Credit group have been ready to move amendments ever since the motion was made for second reading of the

bill, if they could have only got the floor. The reason they were not able to get the floor is that the C.C.F. happens to have a few more members in the house than the Social Crediters, and consequently they have priority in the matter of being recognized. The Conservatives, as the official opposition, are recognized first by Mr. Speaker, as they should be; the spokesman for the C.C.F. is recognized second by Mr. Speaker, which is as it should be, and the Social Crediters have to wait until the others finish their show before they can commence theirs.
But let not the minister think for one minute that the Social Crediters are not solidly behind everything the C.C.F. people have advocated in this debate, with the exception, as I have said, of the resolution preceding the bill concerning which we disagreed with them because at that time we did not know what sort of measure was going to be introduced and we did not know that the government would refuse to let the bill go before the committee on agriculture and colonization, which is the logical place for it to be examined. Apart from that we have been with the C.C.F. in respect of all the arguments that have been put forward.
As far as I am concerned, and I speak for Lethbridge, I will wager that 98 per cent of all the farmers in the constituency of Lethbridge are solidly against the bill and solidly behind advances on grain in storage on the farms. I have not been able to talk to all of them, but I have talked to enough of them to feel quite safe in making that statement.
There are several matters which I think need to be considered at the present time and to which I should like to give some attention. In the first place I should like to congratulate those on the Liberal side who have spoken on the bill. The hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean (Mr. Bourque) gave a little talk today. There were many things in his speech which did the hon. member credit. He said he believed that the farming population should be kept prosperous, and he said a good many other things with which I am entirely in agreement. They do credit to the hon. member and the constituents who sent him here.
The only difficulty in his talk apparently arose from the fact that the hon. member had been slightly misled by men who should have informed him correctly. How could he, coming from Montreal, have anything like an accurate knowledge of conditions obtaining in the three prairie provinces unless he were told by the men in charge, like the Minister of Trade and Commerce? If the Minister of Trade and Commerce was no more clear and straightforward when talking in the Liberal

caucus than he has been on the floor of the house, I do not blame any Liberal for being completely confused with respect to the whole situation in the three prairie provinces.
Two other hon. Liberal members spoke the other day and asked questions. The hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Cannon) made a speech and another hon. member asked several questions. These men made statements which were honest, fact-facing and sincere. They showed that there was a question in their minds which should be clarified. I appreciate all of these statements and questions greatly and I say once more what has already been said many times, that it is my settled conviction after hearing all that has been said that if the people of Canada from coast to coast and the members of this house all knew the facts they would practically unanimously condemn this bill and unanimously demand cash advances on farm-stored grain.

I am giving my speech now and I will welcome honourable, straightforward questions on anything I have to say. I am going to read a quotation here which will give the house the exact picture of what the United States is doing. I wish to read from an editorial in the Lethbridge Herald of December 5. It does not comment on what is going on in the house, so there is no danger of my being out of order. The editorial reads in part as follows:
Writing of the difference between the wheat marketing situation in Canada and in the United States, the agricultural editor of the Minneapolis Tribune visited Hegina recently and in his paper drew this rather startling contrast:
"Let's compare the difference in prices received by two fanners who raise 5,000 bushels of wheat on 250 acres, one near Bismarck, North Dakota, and the other near Regina, Saskatchewan. I am glad the Minister of Agriculture told us that he had kept wheat on his farm for twelve years. I ask any hon. member, even those who are quite talkative; would you rather see that wheat stored safely on the farm in bins, such as those in which the Minister of Agriculture kept his wheat for twelve years, or would you rather see it lie out on the prairie, or would you rather see it unproduced, in the face of the tremendous shortage of food in the world today? Which would you say was the humanitarian thing to do? Which is the common sense thing to do?
Going on to answer the hon. member's intelligent question, I would say that we should
Grain
make provision so farmers could provide adequate storage on their own farms in which they could put their wheat. Then let us pay them enough on the wheat in store on their farms to enable them to carry on and raise a crop next year. Then next year if we are unable to sell the wheat, let us store that wheat also. There is going to come a day when we will need it. They have had the most terrible storms in Europe that they have had in 100 years, and who knows that the same thing may not be repeated for four or five years? If we Canadians have plenty of grain of all kinds stored on our farms, think of the favoured position we would be in with respect to extending help to those needy people! Common sense dictates that no other course be followed but to preserve that wheat and pay the farmers enough money to enable them to pay their running expenses, buy their machinery and be able to carry on and raise more and more crops until the time comes when we should know whether we want to go on raising wheat or whether we want to turn that land back to grass, back to the Indians so to speak.
The trouble today is that we are facing an emergency. That is what confronts us right now. These farmers must have money with which to pay their bills, to pay for gasoline and oil and all the other things needed to carry on. This question of what to do with the grain is most important. This is one factor to which we must give attention before determining what we are to do in respect of measures like this, the silly bill we have before us now.
There is another matter to which thought ought to be given, and that is the large percentage of what is now the three prairie provinces was examined around 1860 by Captain John Palliser, who solemnly declared that it was unfit for human habitation. That area starts at a point in my constituency not far from Lethbridge, goes up somewhere near Saskatoon, and then down back to part of southwest Manitoba. If you place a map before you and draw that general triangle called the Palliser triangle you will see the amount of the land which Captain John Palliser said was unfit for human habitation. Why? He realized that that area might receive ample rain one year or perhaps two years, and then there would be three, four or five dry years during which even the grasshoppers could hardly live.
Let us bear in mind what the government of those days did. We are not blaming them, but we must remember that around 1890 men who sat here-not in this particular house- said, "Let us put people out there; let us let them take a chance." They advertised that

The amount of wheat which they have grown on the Regina plains and in other areas within the Palliser triangle is absolutely astounding. That grain has all been sold abroad by Canada for good solid cash, foreign exchange.
I am not saying that the farmers who produced that grain made anything out of it. By the time the railroads got through hauling it, by the time the handling charges were paid, by the time their various expenses had been taken care of, many of them did not make very much, and many of them made even less.
The fact that those people are out there in an area which can become almost as dry as a desert for two, three, four or five years, when they might be deprived of everything; the fact that they are out there living under those conditions justifies us in doing everything in our power to help them to make good when they have wheat on hand.
I fear that my time is practically exhausted. There were other things which I wished to say, but I shall say only one more thing.
The latest report from Sir John Boyd Orr, the man who originated FAO, states that the world requires $12 billion worth of goods in order to relieve hungry people. As I said in a former speech, we have not had in previous parliaments men with intelligence and understanding enough to find out how to get those goods to those people who need them. Please the Lord, the time may come when we shall know how to get $12 billion into the hands of the needy people so they can buy up the surplus production which is now being brought into being.
The fact that there is such a colossal need for food certainly ought to impress any hon. member of this house or any person in the country that we should go full speed ahead with production and take whatever measures are necessary to enable our producers to produce and store and go on producing from

year to year, until we are able to decide upon a policy if need be, along some other line.

Ottawa, February 18, 1956.
The Honourable Leslie M. Frost,
Premier of Ontario,
Toronto, Ontario.
My dear Premier:
Since the federal-provincial conference adjourned in October, the federal government has made the fiscal proposals outlined in my letters of January 6 and explained them in some detail early this month to provincial treasury officials. It has also made contingent commitments to recommend to parliament financial participation on a large scale in provincially-administered hospital insurance plans. It has received written comments on the proposals from the premiers of three provinces, which have been studied along with comments and questions received in conversation.
I am enclosing a memorandum from the Minister of Finance giving answers to a number of questions that have been raised by provincial representatives. Some of these answers involve some modest development in the details of the proposals advanced by the federal government in January. In particular the government has decided that it would be in accord with the spirit of the present arrangements and with the special nature of the federal tax on insurance premiums to treat provincial taxes on insurance premiums as not being special corporation taxes within the scope of paragraphs three and five of my letter of January. This will improve the arrangements from the point of view of all provinces.
In view of the suggestion that we should meet again in committee to discuss these fiscal arrangements, I feel it would not be fair to the provincial governments if I failed to indicate at this time that the federal government believes its own fiscal situation in the next few years would not justify adding any substantial further financial commitments beyond those already proposed.
In the replies I have received to my letters of January 6, the premiers of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have expressed regret that the federal government was not able to accept suggestions such as they made for a wider application of the fiscal need principle,
and the premier of Saskatchewan has also indicated that in his view fiscal need has not been given sufficient weight. My colleagues and I feel there is a very substantial recognition of fiscal need involved in the equalization payments we have proposed and also in the high level of returns in these tax fields which we are prepared to guarantee to provincial governments. These are, of course, in addition to the existing statutory subsidies which already make special provision for the fiscal need of the Atlantic provinces. We believe we should all have some experience in the practical operation of these proposals before going on to consider other concepts of fiscal need.
I note that only two of the premiers have suggested a resumption of the conference for the purpose of considering the fiscal proposals. Since our federal responsibilities and commitments are now so heavy that we would not be warranted in making any increases in the basic offer we made in January, it may be that the provincial governments generally would not feel that there would be any advantage to be derived from another meeting to discuss fiscal relations.
If a further meeting in committee is generally desired, we would suggest it be held either on March 2 or March 9 in order that final decisions can be reached before the Minister of Finance completes the preparation of his budget. If, on the other hand, most of the provincial governments see no substantial advantage in a general meeting, Mr. Harris and I would be happy to confer at any time between now and the early part of March with the premier or treasurer of any province wishing individual discussions of particular aspects of the proposals.
I should be grateful to have your views at your earliest convenience.
Yours sincerely,
