speechtext:
Memorandum from the Minister of Finance of Canada in the matter of certain questions raised by provincial governments relative to the federal fiscal proposals of January 6, 1956.
In the course of discussions on the fiscal arrangements between Canada and the provinces advanced by letter of the Prime Minister dated January 6, 1956, certain questions were asked and clarifications requested. The federal government's position relative to these matters is set out in this memorandum.

1.	Royalties and the taxation of income from
certain natural resource industries.
Under present fiscal arrangements, the provinces have not been restricted in the imposition of royalties on natural resources. No specific suggestions have been made for changes in the methods employed and none would seem warranted.
Present procedure gives the provinces a substantial concession in the taxation of the income from mining operations and the income from logging operations. It is proposed that this general position be maintained. The federal government would be willing to undertake, should any province wish, further studies in an endeavour to determine if better formulae for the allocation of profits between the primary and secondary phases of the industries can be devised.
The extension of this special treatment to the petroleum and natural gas industry is not warranted, in our opinion.
2.	Tax on insurance premiums.
Under present arrangements, a full offset against the federal tax is given in a nonrenting province for the insurance premium tax charged by that province. In a renting province, the province has been paid for relinquishment of the corporation tax field and the insurance premium tax is included in that category.
In order to put all provinces on an equal basis in this field and at the same time provide to them a substantial additional source of revenue, the federal government is prepared to allow any province an offset for a tax on insurance premiums. Accordingly provincial taxes of this nature would not be considered corporation taxes for purposes of paragraphs 3 and 5 of the Prime Minister's letter of January 6.
3.	Definition of corporation tax.
The definition of corporation tax included in the present tax rental agreement would not seem to require any changes in substance. There are however two exceptions to it where provinces have requested some liberalization of the terms. These are in relation to the limits on license fees now set at $250 per annum for each corporation, and the gross receipts or gross revenue tax on certain public utility companies now set at 4 per cent in the case of telephone companies and 3 per cent in the case of all others.
The federal government will be prepared to increase the allowable limit on license fees to $400 from $250 as now authorized.
As to the rate of tax on gross receipts or gross revenue of certain public utility companies, we will be prepared to study this in 67509-93i
Dominion-Provincial Relations an effort to determine if some increase in the present rates is justified.
4.	Base year for purposes of equalization.
In the proposals the base year on which calculations are made for purposes of equalization is that taxation year preceding the fiscal year for which payments are to be made. The calculation of payments under the current rental agreements has always been on this principle. In view however of the desirability of placing these payments on as current a basis as possible, the federal government is prepared to calculate these equalization payments on the basis of the current taxation year as is provided for in calculation of proposed tax rental payments. This decision accepts the fact that all payments in a fiscal year will be on the basis of estimates and that some substantial if indeterminate financial cost to Canada is involved in this change.
5.	Fire marshal tax.
The federal government is willing to consider a more flexible policy in this matter providing that the principle of the tax being used for costs of operation is maintained.
6.	Tax on income of non-residents.
The federal government will regard tax revenue from income of non-residents of Canada as being subject to allocation under the proposals.
7.	Withholding tax.
The federal position is that taxes shared with the provinces should be confined to those of a nature normally employed by them. Withholding tax does not come in this category and therefore cannot be included for purposes of provincial sharing.
8.	Sharing of income tax from companies
whose main business is the generating or distributing of electrical energy, gas or steam to the public.
The federal government is prepared to continue these payments for the time being but will not incorporate the provision in any formal agreement entered into.
9.	Deduction of certain corporation income tax revenue losses from the payment due a province.
The federal government will not require the inclusion of this provision in any future arrangements.
10.	Collection agreements.
The federal government will undertake to enter into a suitable agreement to make its facilities available to any province for collection of provincial taxes on personal or corporation income providing that the terms of

Dominion-Provincial Relations the provincial statutes do not differ from those of the federal statute and that the rates imposed are at the standard rates of tax as contained in the proposals.
Any agreement would be on an agency fee basis subject to cancellation on adequate notice by either party.
11.	Formula for allocation of corporate profits between provinces.
The current federal procedures in this will be followed.
12.	Special provision for raising revenue for a provincial health program.
The exceptions contained in the definitions of individual income tax in the present agreements will be carried forward into any new agreement.
13.	Old age security tax.
The federal government's position is as stated in the Prime Minister's letter of January 6, 1956.
The old age security tax is not part of the federal income tax structure proper, and will be excluded from calculations of the provincial share of tax fields and from abatement of federal tax.
14.	Adjustment for changes in definition of income, etc.
Under the proposals it is provided that adjustments will be made for changes in rates and personal exemptions in personal income tax and succession duties. Miscellaneous changes in income definitions, allowances, etc., are most difficult to assess and it is therefore necessary that the adjustments be limited to those as originally set out in the proposals.
15.	Tax credits after expiry of agreement. It is not considered necessary or desirable
that the federal government should limit itself to any specific tax policy beyond the period of any agreement entered into. For the purposes of any province entering into a new tax rental agreement, Canada will be prepared to undertake that at the conclusion of the agreement a renting province will not be placed in a less favourable position than a non-renting province relative to federal tax abatements or credits.
16.	Termination.
It is proposed that the same conditions apply as under the present tax rental agreements.
W. E. Harris Minister of Finance.
Ottawa,
February 18, 1956.
